title: Ordaining trees
hookLine: in Thailand, monks wrap trees in robes to protect forests from logging

cards: A strip of saffron cloth, the color of a monk's robe, is wrapped around the trunk of a big old tree at the edge of a forest in Thailand. Monks chant. Villagers stand around with offerings.
Someone ties the knot. From then on the village speaks of that tree differently, and a logger with a chainsaw may stop and think twice. The tree, they say, has been ordained.
A tree becoming a monk? Today, what that's really doing.

teach.h: A ROBE AROUND A TREE IS A SIGN.
teach.b: First, what the ceremony is for. In parts of Thailand, forests that villages relied on for water, food and shade were being cut down.
Some monks, especially in the countryside, began holding ceremonies that wrap a robe around a tree, sometimes around many trees in a forest. They don't claim a tree can really take the precepts.
It's a sign: this forest is held in the same care as the sangha, and harming it is a serious thing. Second, why it fits the tradition.
The Vinaya already asks monks not to destroy plant life.
And trees run through the Buddha's own story. Tradition places his birth in a garden, under a tree. He woke up under a tree, the one later called the bodhi tree.
The Mahaparinibbana Sutta tells of his passing between twin sala trees. Some suttas close with a plain instruction, in paraphrase: here are the roots of trees, here are empty huts. Meditate.

Third, the cost. Monks who led these ceremonies were sometimes told they were meddling in politics, and some faced pressure for it. Communities have argued over whether this is the sangha's work at all.
Last, an old line from the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation: "As the bee collects nectar and departs without injuring the flower, or its colour or scent, so let a sage dwell in his village."
The ordained tree is that line in cloth. Take what you need, and leave the flower whole.

how: In parts of Thailand, monks and villagers hold tree ordination ceremonies, wrapping trees in saffron cloth with chanting and offerings to mark a forest as protected; some monasteries also plant trees and care for forest land.

practice: Bring to mind a tree you know, the one outside your window, on your street, in a park, from your childhood, and see its bark, its shape, how it moves in wind.
Breathe in, remembering that its leaves breathe this same air; breathe out, and let a little thanks go toward it.

wordCard.voice: Ordaining trees. In Thailand, monks wrap saffron robes around trees to mark a forest as protected, a sign drawn from the Vinaya's care for plant life and the trees of the Buddha's own story. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali rukkha: tree. the suttas send monks to meditate at the roots of trees, rukkhamula.

carryVoice: Your line: the ordained tree. A robe on a trunk, and a whole forest held in care. Same time tomorrow.
